# 🌀 DATA VORTEX 2026

### Rebuilding the Social Engine — the complete two-round build

**Forge-X** · Kunal Choudhary · *Aaruush'26*

**PART 1 · Round 1 · 13–16 September** — `12,360 raw rows → 10,221 analysis rows` · `27 justified repairs` · `45 SQL queries`
**PART 2 · Round 2 · 17–18 September** — `9,000 labelled texts → 7,900 modelled` · `sentiment macro-F1 0.613` · `topic macro-F1 0.805` · `14 tests passing`

</div>

<hr />
<h2>The competition in one minute</h2>
<p>One social platform, two collapsed layers, one rule: <strong>nothing is fabricated,
nothing is hardcoded, every claim must survive its own refutation.</strong> Round 1
handed us a dataset hidden behind a broken website and a dead analytics core;
Round 2 handed us a dead semantic layer and 9,000 labelled texts.</p>

<h2>The result in 30 seconds</h2>
<p>The task: a social platform's data pipeline has collapsed. Recover the dataset
(it is <strong>not</strong> given — it is hidden behind a broken website), clean it, explain
every repair, then rebuild the analytics in SQL.</p>
<p><strong>What we did</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Solved the site puzzle and recovered <code>Dataset 01</code> — <strong>12,360</strong> post rows + <strong>1,500</strong> user rows, provenance-verified against the live site.</li>
<li>Found <strong>10 distinct corruption families</strong>, applied <strong>27 logged repairs</strong>, and closed the row arithmetic exactly: <code>12,360 - 360 duplicate replays - 1,779 empty-text hold-outs = 10,221</code>.</li>
<li>Caught the trap the event buried: the "<strong>midnight posting culture</strong>" is fake — see <a href="#exploratory-analysis">Exploratory analysis</a>.</li>
<li>Built a schema'd SQLite core (PK/FK/CHECK constraints, 2 views, long-form hashtag relation) and answered <strong>12 challenges</strong> with CTEs, <code>NTILE</code>, <code>LAG/LEAD</code>, <code>RANK</code> and windowed aggregates — every output captured live.</li>
<li><strong>Refuted five plausible-sounding findings</strong> with statistics instead of publishing them (<a href="#what-we-tested-and-rejected">§8</a>).</li>
</ul>
<hr />

<hr />
<h2>How the dataset was recovered</h2>
<p>The rulebook says the corrupted dataset "will not be given directly". The site
serves an empty <code>&lt;div&gt;</code> — every guessed data URL (<code>/dataset.csv</code>, <code>/api/data</code>,
<code>/logs</code>) 404s. The logic lives in its JS bundle, so the bundle was read and the
four hints resolved 1:1:</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Rulebook hint</th>
<th>What it pointed at in the bundle</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>"may not reveal everything at first glance"</td>
<td>4 of the 5 dashboard modules are deliberate dead ends rendering <em>"this module cannot be displayed"</em></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>"look closely at the recovery logs … beginning of each line"</td>
<td>SYSTEM LOG lines are prefixed <code>hh:mm:ss  service  …</code>; two of seven name <strong><code>node_07</code></strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>"a message hidden in plain sight"</td>
<td>the italic line under the log panel: <code>last known surviving node: node_07</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>"follow the pattern. Decode the connection. Find the node."</td>
<td><code>help</code> advertises only <code>help/status/scan/logs/clear</code>, but the handler matches free text against <code>(connect\|access\|restore\|reconnect\|link)</code> <strong>and</strong> <code>(node.?0?7\|archive)</code></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>No advertised command can win</strong> — the archive opens only through that regex
branch. Typing:</p>
<pre><code>connect node_07
</code></pre>
<p>unlocks <code>ARCHIVE NODE 07</code>, which serves the two files from <code>/dataset/</code>. An
organiser debug panel at <code>?test=true</code> prints a field literally named
<code>Real path → terminal: connect node_07</code>, independently confirming the route.</p>
<p>📄 Full step-by-step (for the viva): <a href="docs/recovery_walkthrough.md"><code>docs/recovery_walkthrough.md</code></a></p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>Provenance.</strong> Both files are downloaded verbatim. <code>src/verify_source.py</code>
re-fetches them and reports <code>2 matched · 0 mismatched</code>, writing SHA-256s to
<code>output/provenance.json</code>. As a bonus check, the same two CSVs are also embedded
as string literals in the app bundle for the in-browser download buttons — and
they parse to <strong>identical rows</strong> (12,361 and 1,501 incl. header), so we know we
have the real dataset and not a decoy.</p>
</blockquote>
<hr />
<h2>Corruption inventory and repairs</h2>
<p>Profiling came first; every rule below answers a defect that was observed, not a
checklist item. Counts are from <code>data/clean/repair_log.csv</code>.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Defect in the raw intake</th>
<th style="text-align: right;">Rows</th>
<th>Treatment</th>
<th>Justification</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>exact duplicate rows</td>
<td style="text-align: right;"><strong>360</strong></td>
<td>dropped; <code>post_id</code> made a real PK</td>
<td>identical across all 8 fields = outage retry replay</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>negative <code>likes</code></td>
<td style="text-align: right;"><strong>525</strong></td>
<td><code>abs()</code> restore, row-flagged</td>
<td>mirrored distribution, one column only (see <a href="#the-two-decisions-that-needed-proof">the proof section</a>)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>likes</code> as float strings (<code>-1205.0</code>)</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">525</td>
<td>cast to nullable <code>Int64</code></td>
<td>keeps NULL ≠ 0</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>blank / <code>NULL</code> likes</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">1,858</td>
<td>real NULL, <strong>never imputed</strong></td>
<td>fabrication is prohibited</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>blank / <code>NULL</code> platform</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">1,846</td>
<td>explicit <code>Unspecified</code> bucket</td>
<td>not an invented platform</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>blank or <code>NULL</code> text body</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">1,779</td>
<td>held out to a separate CSV</td>
<td>count must reconcile</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>injected <code>&lt;br&gt;</code> / <code>&lt;div&gt;</code></td>
<td style="text-align: right;">663</td>
<td>markup stripped, text kept</td>
<td>renderer artefact</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>trailing <code>&amp;amp;</code> entity</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">341</td>
<td>unescaped, orphaned <code>&amp;</code>/<code>,</code> trimmed</td>
<td>layered corruption</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>double-encoded UTF-8 (<code>C3 A9</code>)</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">316</td>
<td>latin-1 round-trip reversed</td>
<td>see <a href="#the-two-decisions-that-needed-proof">the proof section</a></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>three timestamp formats</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">4,805 / 3,669 / 3,526</td>
<td>one UTC datetime, ambiguity flagged</td>
<td>see <a href="#the-two-decisions-that-needed-proof">the proof section</a></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Reconciliation</strong> — the single most auditable line in this submission:</p>
<pre><code>12,360 raw  -  360 exact duplicates  -  1,779 empty-text hold-outs  =  10,221 analysis rows
</code></pre>
<p>Held-out rows are written to <code>data/clean/Social_Engine_Posts_EmptyText_HeldOut.csv</code>
rather than deleted, so the identity closes from files on disk.</p>
<hr />
<h2>The two decisions that needed proof</h2>
<p><strong>Day-first dates.</strong> <code>timestamp</code> holds ISO-8601, epoch-seconds <strong>and</strong>
<code>dd-mm-yyyy</code>. For that last block, <code>MM-DD</code> vs <code>DD-MM</code> is settled arithmetically:</p>
<pre><code>of the 3,622 raw dd-mm-yyyy rows:
   first field  &gt; 12 :  2,172      &lt;- a day
   second field &gt; 12 :      0      &lt;- a month can never be 25
</code></pre>
<p>Month-first is impossible for most of the block, so one convention (day-first)
is applied to all of it; mixing readings per row would invent a distribution. The
1,450 rows where both fields are ≤ 12 are genuinely ambiguous — all flagged with
<code>flag_ambiguous_date_format</code>, and no claim in this repo depends on them.</p>
<p><strong>Negative likes are a sign flip, not lost data.</strong></p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th style="text-align: right;">count</th>
<th style="text-align: right;">median</th>
<th style="text-align: right;">max</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>positive <code>likes</code></td>
<td style="text-align: right;">9,976</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">2,505</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">5,000</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>|negative <code>likes</code>|</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">525</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">2,388</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">4,987</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><code>likes</code> is the <em>only</em> numeric column with negatives (<code>shares</code>, <code>comments</code> have
zero), every negative carries a <code>.0</code> suffix while positives are bare integers,
and the negatives mirror the positives' distribution and their 5,000 ceiling.
Lost data would be <em>missing</em>, not a mirror image — so magnitude is restored and
every row flagged. <code>RESTORE_SIGN_FLIPPED_LIKES = False</code> in <code>src/config.py</code>
switches to the conservative reading (null them) and the pipeline still runs.</p>
<p>📄 All 10 rules with reasoning: <a href="docs/cleaning_decisions.md"><code>docs/cleaning_decisions.md</code></a></p>
<hr />
<h2>Exploratory analysis</h2>
<h3>The finding that matters most: the midnight peak does not exist</h3>
<p>A naive hour-of-day histogram on the <strong>cleaned</strong> table shows <strong>3,325 posts at
00:00 = 32.53%</strong> of the corpus — an impressive "night-owl community" signal.</p>
<p>It is entirely an artefact. <strong>3,002 of those rows come from the <code>dd-mm-yyyy</code>
intake block, which carries a date but no clock.</strong> Restricted to rows that
genuinely have a time, the busiest hour holds <strong>4.63%</strong> against a trough of
3.80% — a spread ratio of 1.22. There is no circadian pattern; there is a
serialisation bug.</p>
<p>The <code>has_time</code> guard is therefore carried <strong>into the SQL schema</strong>, not just the
cleaning script, so no downstream query can repeat the mistake.</p>
<p><img alt="naive vs valid hour-of-day" src="output/figures/03_time.png" /></p>
<h3>Volume is flat, so the story is not growth</h3>
<p><img alt="monthly volume vs engagement" src="output/figures/01_trend.png" /></p>
<p>Monthly volume mean 852, population SD 24.5; z-scores run -2.36 (2025-02) to
+1.07 (2024-05) with 3 of 12 months beyond ±1 SD. That oscillates around a flat
mean — no monotone component, so "the platform is growing" is unsupported.</p>
<h3>Platform differences are inside the noise band</h3>
<p><img alt="platform comparison" src="output/figures/02_platform.png" /></p>
<p>Mean likes vary just <strong>3.8%</strong> across the five real platforms, and the rate at
which likes went missing is near-identical everywhere (14.16% Reddit → 15.67%
Twitter). That uniformity is the evidence that corruption hit the <strong>transport
layer, not the sampling</strong> — which is what licenses pooling platforms at all.
<code>Unspecified</code> (15.08%) is shown as its own grey bar, never hidden inside a rate.</p>
<h3>Users: reach ≠ resonance</h3>
<p><img alt="followers vs engagement" src="output/figures/07_users.png" /></p>
<p>Follower count vs mean per-post engagement is <strong>r = -0.0433</strong> (r² = 0.19%) — and
the follower-quintile view (centre) is flat, which proves that's a real null and
not a missed non-linearity. Top decile of authors holds 18.4% of total
engagement, driven by volume, not by per-post quality.</p>
<p><img alt="sentiment mix" src="output/figures/05_sentiment.png" /></p>
<p>Corpus leans positive (40.95% / 31.91% neutral / 27.14% negative on a published
keyword lexicon — chosen over a model so any row can be recomputed by hand), but
correlation with likes is r = -0.0142. Negative posts even average slightly
<em>more</em> likes (2,509.8 vs 2,454.8) — the classic complaint-gets-engagement shape,
at an r that must honestly be reported as <strong>no relationship</strong>.</p>
<hr />
<h2>The SQL analytical core</h2>
<p><code>output/social_engine.db</code>, built by <code>src/build_db.py</code>: <code>posts</code>, <code>users</code>,
<code>post_tags</code> with <strong>primary keys, a foreign key, <code>CHECK</code> constraints and four
indices</strong>, plus <code>v_posts_enriched</code> / <code>v_monthly</code> views. Schema choices encode
reasoning rather than describing it — e.g. <code>CHECK (likes IS NULL OR likes &gt;= 0)</code>
puts the domain rule in the database, and <code>platform</code> is a <code>CHECK</code>-enumerated set
so a future bad export fails at INSERT instead of becoming a sixth platform.</p>
<p><strong>12 challenges, all executing</strong>, across the four named categories:</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Trend detection</strong></td>
<td>Q1 momentum + z-score vs the series' own SD · Q2 centred moving average and inflection points · Q10 hashtag momentum on share-of-month</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Anomaly discovery</strong></td>
<td>Q4 ratio-based amplification anomalies · Q5 Poisson attribution test · Q11 gap-and-islands posting streaks</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Behavioural grouping</strong></td>
<td>Q3 platform league table with missingness exposed · Q7 rank-based RFM · Q12 integrity gate</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Correlation</strong></td>
<td>Q8 Pearson r assembled from raw sums · Q9 the same relation bucketed</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Uses CTEs, <code>NTILE</code>, <code>LAG/LEAD</code>, <code>RANK</code>, <code>SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER ()</code>, <code>ROWS BETWEEN</code>,
views — as the rulebook invites.</p>

  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="820" alt="Q5 Poisson attribution test"/>
</p>

<p><strong>Q5 is the query we're proudest of</strong>, and it's the one that <em>removes</em> a finding
(see <a href="#what-we-tested-and-rejected">What we tested and rejected</a>). Two traps are documented in the SQL itself: SQL's bare <code>+</code> is
NULL-propagating, so <code>AVG(likes+shares+comments)</code> would silently drop 1,532 rows
and change the population and the metric at once — hence <code>COALESCE</code> in a view,
defined once.</p>
<p>📄 Design rationale + SQLite↔Postgres dialect notes: <a href="docs/schema_design.md"><code>docs/schema_design.md</code></a>
📄 Every query, its logic and its live output: <a href="output/sql_outputs.md"><code>output/sql_outputs.md</code></a></p>

<p>**<p align="center">
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="520" alt="engagement by location (the M1 ranking and its volume trap)"/>
</p></p>
<p>Three things in this set are worth more than the answers.**</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>H1 returns zero rows, and that is the answer.</strong> The 2× bar is
  7,247.43 against a best user average of
  6,545.50. Rather than reach for a friendlier
  definition, the query prints its own baseline and threshold, proves the gap is
  arithmetic, and adds a threshold ladder so the reader can see where the
  question <em>does</em> have an answer.</li>
<li><strong>M5 is a trap with a price tag.</strong> 2,201 "anomalies"
  appear if a blank like count is read as zero; 1,154
  of them exist only because the field is missing, and the reconciliation query
  proves the arithmetic gap equals that count exactly.</li>
<li><strong>H5 cannot be asked of the cleaned table.</strong> Cleaning is the step that removed
  the corruption, so the anomalies are detected on a verbatim staging table of
  the 12,360 intake rows, using the same SQL predicate that populated the
  inventory. The per-family counts match the Phase-1 corruption log exactly.</li>
</ul>
<p>Six findings were produced and then <strong>rejected by their own companions</strong>: the
platform leader (E1b), the platform ranking (E3b), the follower advantage (M2b),
the location ranking (M1b), the over-sharing alarm (M5b) and the 2× power users
(H1b/H1c). They are listed in full in
<a href="output/Phase2_ChallengeSet_Report.pdf">the report</a> — the rejections are the work.</p>

<h2>What we tested and rejected</h2>
<p>The most useful thing a data engineer does is kill their own nice-looking
findings. All five were plausible and all five failed:</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Tempting claim</th>
<th>Verdict</th>
<th>How it was refuted</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>"Night-owl audience — a third of posts at midnight"</td>
<td><strong>Artefact</strong></td>
<td>3,002 of 3,325 are date-only rows; real peak is 4.63% (Q6)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>"A coordinated amplification ring is gaming engagement"</td>
<td><strong>Not a ring</strong></td>
<td>846 anomalous posts tested against a Poisson null (λ = n_anom/n_users): observed 31 vs 29.6 expected, <strong>O/E = 1.05 → diffuse</strong> (Q5)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>"Bigger audiences engage more"</td>
<td><strong>Null</strong></td>
<td>r = -0.0433, and flat across follower quintiles — a real null, not a missed curve (Q8/Q9)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>"Sentiment drives engagement"</td>
<td><strong>Null</strong></td>
<td>r = -0.0142</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>"Instagram/YouTube outperform"</td>
<td><strong>Noise</strong></td>
<td>3.8% spread, uniform missingness across platforms</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Q5 is the one to defend: <strong>a per-user leaderboard would have "found" a bot ring
in any diffuse anomaly.</strong> Testing the tail against chance is what stops a
fabricated insight from reaching the report — and the negative result is
published as a negative result.</p>
<p align="center">
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="520" alt="the 846 amplification anomalies — diffuse across users, not a ring (Q4/Q5)"/>
</p>

<hr />
<h2>Assumptions and limitations</h2>
<p>Stated up front because "clearly explain assumptions" is a scored criterion:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Single naive timezone.</strong> No offset exists anywhere in the file; UTC assumed.
  If one is supplied later, only <code>post_hour</code> moves — no count changes.</li>
<li><strong>1,450 dates stay genuinely ambiguous</strong> (day ≤ 12 and month ≤ 12). Flagged,
  not hidden; any result can be recomputed on the unambiguous subset.</li>
<li><strong><code>abs()</code> on likes is a repair, not an imputation.</strong> One config flag reverses
  it; it affects 525 raw rows, 430 of which survive into the analysis table.</li>
<li><strong>Nothing is imputed.</strong> 1,532 likes remain NULL and are excluded per metric.</li>
<li><strong>Sentiment is a published keyword lexicon</strong>, not a model — deliberately, so
  any single row can be verified by hand.</li>
<li><strong>Held-out ≠ deleted.</strong> 1,779 empty-body rows stay on disk so the arithmetic closes.</li>
<li>We cannot validate against the organisers' reference "true" dataset; our
  standard is that every repair is justified by evidence <em>in</em> the file.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Round 2 in 30 seconds</h2>
<p>The task: Round 1 rebuilt the structured analytics. Now the engine "still
struggles to understand the meaning, tone, and intent behind human language
because its semantic comprehension layer has failed." Dataset 2 — 9,000
labelled social-media texts — must teach it again, with the full trail the
rulebook demands: preprocessing, model selection, training methodology,
evaluation, confusion matrix, error analysis.</p>
<p><strong>What we did</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Audited Dataset 2 and closed the row arithmetic exactly:
  <code>9,000 raw − 0 empty − 1,100 exact duplicates = 7,900 modelled</code> — duplicates
  are <strong>held out, not deleted</strong> (Round 1 doctrine: the count must reconcile).</li>
<li>One stratified 80/20 split (<code>sentiment × topic</code>, seed 42 → <strong>6,320 / 1,580</strong>)
  shared by both tasks; the test set is touched <strong>exactly once</strong>, by the CV winner.</li>
<li>Ran a <strong>6-specification bake-off</strong> per task (dummy · Naive Bayes · LogReg ·
  LinearSVC · word-only TF-IDF · word+char TF-IDF union) under 5-fold
  stratified CV, all grids declared up front in <code>src/round2/config.py</code>:
  <strong><code>logreg_union</code></strong> wins sentiment (margin +0.0081 over <code>svc_union</code>),
  <strong><code>svc_union</code></strong> wins topic (+0.0134 over <code>logreg_union</code>) and is wrapped in
  sigmoid calibration so it outputs honest probabilities.</li>
<li>Test results — sentiment: <strong>acc 0.6133 · macro-F1 0.6134 · ROC-AUC OvR 0.792</strong>;
  topic: <strong>acc 0.9677 · macro-F1 0.8051 · MCC 0.864</strong>.</li>
<li>Read the errors instead of averaging them: the topic "gap" is pure
  sample-size arithmetic (two rare classes at n=26 and n=50), and sentiment's
  confusion is a Neg↔Neu story — see <a href="#error-analysis-reading-the-mistakes">Error analysis</a>.</li>
<li>Ran the unsupervised cross-check the task invites, watched it <strong>fail</strong>
  (NMI ≈ 0.002), and published the failure — see
  <a href="#the-unsupervised-cross-check-that-failed-and-is-published-anyway">the honest section</a>.</li>
<li>Shipped all four rulebook deliverables, checksummed for the form.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<h2>Reproduce it — Round 2</h2>

pip install -r requirements-round2.txt
./run_round2.sh
</code></pre>

<p>Deterministic: <strong>one seed (42) drives the split, the CV folds, the calibration
and LDA/NMF</strong>; no network, no GPU, no sampling at run time. <code>src/round2/predict.py</code>
loads any shipped <code>.pkl</code> and scores raw text from the command line:</p>
<pre><code class="language-bash">python src/round2/predict.py --task sentiment --text &quot;updates broke my login again&quot;
python src/round2/predict.py --task topic      --text &quot;updates broke my login again&quot;
</code></pre>
<hr />
<h2>The dataset and the intake decisions</h2>
<p>Four columns: <code>text_id</code>, <code>post_text</code>, <code>sentiment_label</code>, <code>topic_category</code>.
The pipeline <strong>refuses to run on any other schema</strong> rather than silently
misreading columns (decision D1).</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Intake fact</th>
<th style="text-align: right;">Value</th>
<th>Decision</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>raw rows</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">9,000</td>
<td>—</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>empty texts</td>
<td style="text-align: right;"><strong>0</strong></td>
<td>nothing to hold out (Round 1 had 1,779)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>exact duplicate texts</td>
<td style="text-align: right;"><strong>1,100</strong></td>
<td>held out, keep-first — see below</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>conflicting labels on the same text</td>
<td style="text-align: right;"><strong>0</strong></td>
<td>the noisy case the pipeline was built to surface never occurs</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>modelled rows</strong></td>
<td style="text-align: right;"><strong>7,900</strong></td>
<td>the arithmetic closes on files on disk</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<pre><code> 9,000 raw  -  0 empty-text  -  1,100 exact duplicates  =  7,900 modelled rows
                               split:  6,320 train  /  1,580 test   (id overlap: 0)
</code></pre>
<p><strong>Why duplicates are held out, not dropped-and-forgotten (D4).</strong> A duplicate
straddling the split is an answer sheet in the training data — it inflates
scores without buying generalisation. Keep-first quarantines them to
<code>data/round2/clean/exact_duplicate_heldout.csv</code>, so the identity closes from
files on disk. The genuinely noisy case — the same text with <em>conflicting</em>
labels — is label noise, and deleting disagreement would hide it, so the
pipeline keeps conflicts everywhere and reports them. The data contained none.</p>
<p><strong>Class balance decides the metric.</strong> Sentiment is near-perfectly balanced
(2,430 / 2,748 / 2,722 across Neg / Neu / Pos after hold-outs). Topics are not:</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th style="text-align: right;">Community_Discussion</th>
<th style="text-align: right;">Technical_Issues</th>
<th style="text-align: right;">Feature_Feedback</th>
<th style="text-align: right;">Account_Security</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: right;">6,803</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">718</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">250</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">129</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>That is a <strong>53 : 1</strong> imbalance, which is why <strong>macro-F1 is the headline
metric</strong> everywhere in Round 2: a majority-class classifier scores 0.86
accuracy on topic while learning nothing (macro-F1 0.24 — see
<a href="#what-we-tested-and-rejected--round-2">What we tested and rejected</a>).</p>
<p>Text lengths run 24–158 chars (mean 106.5) — genuinely short text, which
shapes every feature decision below.</p>
<p align="center">
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="420" alt="label distributions: balanced sentiment, 53:1 topic imbalance"/>
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="420" alt="text length distribution, 24-158 chars"/>
</p>

<hr />
<h2>Preprocessing: conservative by design</h2>
<p><code>src/round2/text_clean.py</code> does the minimum that helps and nothing that
destroys signal: HTML unescaping, URL/email masking, lowercasing, elongation
collapsing (<code>sooo</code> → <code>soo</code>), whitespace repair. Slang, punctuation and
deliberate misspellings <strong>are</strong> sentiment on social media — aggressive
stemming or stop-word nuking would erase them.</p>
<p><strong>Features (D8) — the one union that matters:</strong></p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>view</th>
<th>n-grams</th>
<th>why</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>word</td>
<td>(1, 2), <code>min_df=2</code>, sublinear TF</td>
<td>carries semantics and negation bigrams ("not working")</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>char</td>
<td><code>char_wb</code> (3, 5)</td>
<td>robust to typos, elongations and slang ("gr8", "luv") that word tokenisers shatter</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>union</strong></td>
<td>both, concatenated</td>
<td>measured effect in the bake-off: <strong>+0.020</strong> sentiment, <strong>+0.176</strong> topic CV macro-F1 over word-only</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><code>min_df=2</code> drops one-off misspellings from the vocabulary; topics modelled
unsupervised get unigrams only (D9 — bigrams made topics measurably noisier).</p>
<hr />
<h2>Model selection: a bake-off, not a guess</h2>
<p>Six specifications per task, scored by <strong>5-fold stratified CV on the train
split only</strong> (<code>f1_macro</code>, D6). Grids are small and declared up front (D7) —
the point is a defensible comparison, not a grid-search trophy.</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Sentiment spec</th>
<th>CV macro-F1</th>
<th>Topic spec</th>
<th>CV macro-F1</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>dummy (most-frequent)</td>
<td>0.3240 ± 0.007</td>
<td>dummy</td>
<td>0.2397 ± 0.011</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Naive Bayes · word</td>
<td>0.5709 ± 0.012</td>
<td>Naive Bayes · word</td>
<td>0.3768 ± 0.045</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>LogReg · word</td>
<td>0.5915 ± 0.016</td>
<td>LogReg · word</td>
<td>0.5791 ± 0.028</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>LinearSVC · word</td>
<td>0.5893 ± 0.014</td>
<td>LinearSVC · word</td>
<td>0.6042 ± 0.036</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>LogReg · word+char ← winner</strong></td>
<td><strong>0.6110 ± 0.015</strong></td>
<td>LogReg · word+char</td>
<td>0.7666 ± 0.034</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>LinearSVC · word+char</td>
<td>0.6028 ± 0.009</td>
<td><strong>LinearSVC · word+char ← winner</strong></td>
<td><strong>0.7800 ± 0.037</strong></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p align="center">
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="420" alt="sentiment CV bake-off"/>
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="420" alt="topic CV bake-off"/>
</p>

<p><strong>Why linear models, and no transformer (D7).</strong> ~9k short texts do not justify
a GPU model; TF-IDF + linear classifiers reproduce on any machine in seconds,
and their feature weights are inspectable line-by-line in a viva. The
char-ngram union is what buys the gains above — visible in the table, not
asserted. The winner margins are reported honestly: sentiment's top two differ
by <strong>+0.0081</strong>, inside the ±0.015 fold noise band, so the shipped choice is
"CV winner", not "proved superior".</p>
<p><strong>Calibration (D10).</strong> A LinearSVC ranks but doesn't emit probabilities, so
the topic winner is wrapped in sigmoid calibration (3-fold). The metrics PDF
reports whether calibration helped or hurt log-loss rather than assuming.</p>
<p align="center">
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="420" alt="sentiment reliability diagram"/>
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="420" alt="topic reliability diagram after sigmoid calibration"/>
</p>

<hr />
<h2>Training methodology</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>One seed (42)</strong> drives the split, the CV folds, the calibration and
  LDA/NMF — declared in <code>src/round2/config.py</code> before anything ran.</li>
<li><strong>Selection lives inside train.</strong> Hyperparameters are chosen by CV on the
  6,320 training rows; the 1,580-row test set is scored <strong>once</strong> by each refit
  winner (D5/D6). No test peeking, no seed hacking.</li>
<li><strong>Stratification</strong> on <code>sentiment × topic</code> (backing off to sentiment-only if a
  combo has &lt; 2 rows) keeps the rare classes represented in test:
  Account_Security n=26, Feature_Feedback n=50.</li>
<li><strong>Total cost: 273 s on CPU</strong>, of which LDA takes 13.9 s and NMF 0.5 s.
  Every analyst decision is a named constant (D1–D10) in one config file, so a
  judge can change an assumption and re-run the whole thing in one place.</li>
</ul>
<p align="center">
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="420" alt="sentiment learning curves: CV score vs training size"/>
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="420" alt="topic learning curves: CV score vs training size"/>
</p>

<hr />
<h2>Error analysis: reading the mistakes</h2>
<p><strong>The topic "gap" is sample-size arithmetic, not model failure.</strong> The two rare
classes have <em>perfect precision</em> and recall 0.44 / 0.50 — the model finds them
only when the vocabulary is unambiguous. Check the arithmetic:</p>
<pre><code>(0.982 + 0.961 + 0.611 + 0.667) / 4  =  0.805   ← the macro-F1 &quot;gap&quot; is the tail
</code></pre>
<p>With the head at 0.982 / 0.961, no model choice moves the mean much; fixing it
needs more labelled tail data or threshold tuning — and class-weighting was
already inside the CV comparison. The Evaluation Metrics Report breaks the
same errors out by text length, by class and by confidence slice:</p>
<p align="center">
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="420" alt="sentiment error slices by length, class and confidence"/>
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="420" alt="topic error slices by length, class and confidence"/>
</p>

<p><strong>Sentiment's confusion is Neg↔Neu.</strong> Neutral is the catch-all class
(precision 0.565, recall 0.519): factual-sounding complaints land in Neutral;
hedged positives stay Positive. Meanwhile ROC-AUC OvR = <strong>0.792</strong> — the
<em>ranking</em> signal is real, the 3-class decision boundary is what blurs. That is
the classic short-text sentiment ceiling, and it sets up Round 3 honestly.</p>
<p align="center">
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="420" alt="sentiment ROC, one-vs-rest"/>
  <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="420" alt="topic ROC, one-vs-rest"/>
</p>

<h2>The unsupervised cross-check that failed (and is published anyway)</h2>
<p>The dataset invites topic modelling, so LDA and NMF were fitted with K=4 (one
topic per labelled class) as an unsupervised sanity check against the human
labels:</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>model</th>
<th style="text-align: right;">NMI</th>
<th style="text-align: right;">ARI</th>
<th style="text-align: right;">fit time</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>LDA</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">0.0020</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">−0.0030</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">13.9 s</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>NMF</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">0.0027</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">0.0068</td>
<td style="text-align: right;">0.5 s</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><strong>Near-zero agreement.</strong> The labelled topics do not fall out of raw
co-occurrence statistics — <code>Community_Discussion</code> is largely defined by the
<em>absence</em> of the other topics' vocabulary, which is exactly the kind of class
co-occurrence cannot find. Two consequences, both kept:</p>
<ol>
<li>the semantic layer ships <strong>supervised</strong>, with this disagreement stated in
   the report rather than buried; and</li>
<li>what the unsupervised topics <em>did</em> latch onto is shown below — evidence,
   not embarrassment. Their top words have nothing to say about security or
   feedback; the agreement chart puts numbers on the disagreement.</li>
</ol>

<hr />
<h2>What we tested and rejected — Round 2</h2>
<p>Round 1 killed five findings with statistics; Round 2 killed five modelling
shortcuts the same way. All five were tempting, all five failed:</p>
<table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Tempting claim</th>
<th>Verdict</th>
<th>How it was refuted</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>"Naive Bayes — the classic text baseline — will do"</td>
<td><strong>Beaten</strong></td>
<td>CV macro-F1 0.571 vs 0.611 (sentiment), 0.377 vs 0.780 (topic) — its independence assumption pays no rent on n-gram features</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>"Word n-grams are enough for short posts"</td>
<td><strong>+char wins</strong></td>
<td>word-only → union: <strong>+0.020</strong> sentiment, <strong>+0.176</strong> topic — the slang and typos live in characters</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>"Unsupervised LDA will rediscover the four labelled topics"</td>
<td><strong>Refuted</strong></td>
<td>NMI 0.0020, ARI −0.0030 — published as a finding, not hidden</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>"Accuracy is the metric to beat"</td>
<td><strong>Trap</strong></td>
<td>the majority-class dummy scores <strong>0.86 accuracy</strong> on topic with <strong>0.240 macro-F1</strong> — accuracy hides the tail the rubric cares about</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>"Pick a family and tune harder"</td>
<td><strong>Noise</strong></td>
<td>sentiment's top two specs sit 0.0081 apart, inside ±0.015 fold noise — the margin is reported, not celebrated</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>The honest positive result: calibrated linear models over TF-IDF unions are
<strong>sufficient</strong> for the head classes (F1 ≥ 0.96 on both large topic classes),
and the residual error is a <em>data</em> limitation (25% of test tail mass sits in
classes with ≤ 50 examples) — stated as a limitation, not spun as a win.</p>
<hr />
<h2>Repo structure (the Round 2 slice)</h2>
<pre><code>data/round2/raw/    Dataset2.csv -- 9,000 labelled texts, byte-identical to the
                    official download (MD5-verified before anything ran)
data/round2/clean/  profile.json · split_manifest.json · cleaning_report.md ·
                    train/test CSVs · exact_duplicate_heldout.csv
src/round2/         config.py (all analyst decisions D1–D10) · data · text_clean
                    models · train · evaluate · figures · predict
                    build_eval_report · build_tech_report · make_notebook
                    make_submission
models/round2/      sentiment_best.pkl · topic_best.pkl (calibrated) ·
                    topic_lda.pkl · topic_nmf.pkl
notebooks/          02_nlp_rebuild_semantic_layer.ipynb -- executed, outputs attached
output/round2/      metrics.json · train_record.json · figures/ (19 PNGs) ·
                    Evaluation_Metrics_Report.pdf · Round2_Technical_Report.pdf
tests/              test_round2.py -- 14 invariant tests
submission/round2_form_upload/   the Google Form set: Slot1–4 + checksums
</code></pre>
<p>The form takes <strong>one file per slot, max 10 MB</strong>, so the four <code>.pkl</code> models are
bundled into a single <code>Slot2_Trained_Model_Files.zip</code> (5.0 MB) inside
<a href="submission/round2_form_upload/SUBMISSION_DETAILS.md"><code>submission/round2_form_upload/</code></a>;
<code>SUBMISSION_DETAILS.md</code> carries the SHA-256 of every upload so what gets
submitted is provably what this repo ships. Everything regenerates from
<code>./run_round2.sh</code>.</p>
<hr />
<h2>Assumptions and limitations — Round 2</h2>
<p>Stated up front because "clearly explain assumptions" is a scored criterion:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Duplicates are held out, conflicts would be kept.</strong> 1,100 exact duplicates
  quarantined; the conflicting-label case (label noise) would be kept and
  reported — the data contained none (0 conflicts).</li>
<li><strong>One split, one seed, one test touch.</strong> All selection happens inside the
  train folds; test is scored once. Any reported number is reproducible from
  <code>config.py</code> + <code>./run_round2.sh</code> alone.</li>
<li><strong>Linear models over deep nets, on purpose</strong> — the alternatives were measured
  (see the bake-off), not assumed away. The ROC-AUC 0.792 / accuracy 0.613 gap
  on sentiment marks where a transformer would plausibly help; that is a
  stated future step, not a hidden weakness.</li>
<li><strong>Macro-F1 is the headline</strong> because the topic classes are imbalanced 53:1;
  accuracy would flatter a majority-class classifier by 0.15.</li>
<li><strong>Calibration is sigmoid, 3-fold</strong>, chosen to keep the SVC honest about
  probabilities; its effect on log-loss is reported both ways.</li>
<li><strong>No external embeddings, no LLM features, no network</strong> — the whole pipeline
  is offline, CPU-only and deterministic from one seed.</li>
<li>The tail classes (n=26 / n=50 in test) are small enough that their per-class
  recall carries real variance; the report quotes them with support counts
  attached, never naked.</li>
</ul>

<div align="center">
